advisor.summary: On a seller-financed property sale, §453 recognizes gain as payments arrive — gross profit ratio times each principal payment — rather than stacking the entire gain into the closing year. Spread over several years, more of the gain rides the 0%/15% capital-gain brackets and stays under the net investment income tax threshold; that spread is the source of the modeled benefit. Two statutory exceptions do most of the damage in bad plans: §453(i) forces all depreciation recapture into income in the sale year regardless of cash received, and §453A charges interest on the deferred tax once large-balance thresholds are crossed. Installment treatment is automatic; electing out under §453(d) is the affirmative choice when one-year recognition is actually cheaper. The engine models an even spread of the elected gain over the note term; recapture, note interest, and §453A charges sit outside the model and belong in the plan narrative.
mechanics: Each year’s recognized gain equals the gross profit ratio (gross profit over total contract price) times the principal collected; stated interest on the note is ordinary income, and §§483 and 1274 impute interest when the note carries an inadequate rate.

Bracket smoothing drives the value: several mid-size gain slices can sit inside the 15% bracket and under the net investment income tax threshold, where single-year recognition would stack into the top capital-gain rate plus surtax.

§453(i) pulls all depreciation recapture into the year of sale even if little cash changed hands — the down payment must be sized to cover that tax, and heavily depreciated property (post cost segregation) can make the year-one bill dominant.

§453A levies an interest charge on the deferred tax where aggregate installment obligations from large sales exceed $5 million outstanding at year end, and pledging the note as loan collateral accelerates gain.

Related-party sales carry the §453(e) tripwire — the buyer’s resale within two years accelerates the seller’s deferred gain — and dealer property and publicly traded securities are ineligible outright.
The model spreads the entered gain evenly across the note term starting in the sale year; it does not model recapture, interest income, or buyer-default scenarios.

authority.note: The installment method — proportional recognition as payments arrive, automatic unless the taxpayer elects out under (d).
All depreciation recapture is ordinary income in the year of disposition whatever the payment schedule — the year-one liquidity driver.
Interest charge on the deferred tax for large installment balances, plus the pledge-acceleration rule.
A related-party resale within two years accelerates the deferred gain.
Imputed-interest and OID rules — the note must bear adequate stated interest or payments are recharacterized.
The installment reporting vehicle for the sale year and every collection year.

requirements: A non-dealer disposition of real property with at least one payment arriving after the year of sale.
A written note at or above the applicable federal rate, with a genuine amortization schedule and recorded security.
A down payment large enough to cover the year-one tax on recaptured depreciation plus closing costs.
A buyer whose credit the client has genuinely underwritten — the seller is now the lender.
risks: Buyer default is the dominant economic risk: repossession under §1038 returns the property but rarely the plan, and a failed note can swamp the tax savings — no marquee tax case exists here because the losses are commercial, not doctrinal.
A thin down payment against heavy recapture leaves a year-one tax bill with no cash to pay it — the classic malpractice pattern on post-cost-segregation dispositions.
Deferred gain is taxed at future years’ rates and thresholds — rate risk cuts both ways and should be disclosed, not assumed away.
Balances above the $5 million threshold accrue the §453A interest charge and erode the deferral’s value.
An installment note gets no basis step-up at death — the deferred gain passes to the heirs as income in respect of a decedent, unlike the property itself had it been held.
stateNotes: Conformity: nearly all states conform to federal installment reporting through their federal starting point, but a seller who moves states mid-note pays each collection year under the residence rules then in force — multistate sequencing matters.
Missouri conforms via federal AGI (RSMo §143.121); Missouri-source gain collected by a nonresident seller stays Missouri-source in every collection year.

PTET interaction: none for a personally held rental — no PTET issue arises unless the property sits in an electing pass-through, in which case the entity-level recognition schedule drives the PTET base year by year.
reviewChecklist: Both-ways projection — full recognition vs. installment spread — in the file, including net investment income tax thresholds and bracket breakpoints.
Recapture computed separately, with the down payment confirmed to cover the year-one tax.
Note papered at an adequate rate and secured; §453A exposure and any related-party buyer flagged.
Form 6252 calendared for the sale year and every collection year.
Client advised in writing on default risk and the missing basis step-up on the note.

client.teaser: Spread the tax on a property sale over the years you collect the money.
client.headline: Sell now, pay tax as the money comes in
plainEnglish: Sell a property for a big profit and take all the cash at once, and the whole gain lands in one tax year. That often pushes you into the top capital-gain rate plus an extra surtax. Lumpy income is costly income.

With an installment sale, the buyer pays you over several years, and you pay tax only as money arrives. Each year’s slice is smaller, so more of it is taxed at lower rates. You also earn interest from the buyer along the way — you are the bank.

Two things need planning. First, tax on your past depreciation is due in year one no matter what, so the down payment must cover it. Second, you are trusting the buyer to keep paying, so the note needs real security. We build in both protections before you sign.
client.analogy: Think of your gain as water and the tax brackets as measuring cups. Pour it all at once and it overflows into the priciest cup. Pour it over five years and each cup stays in the cheap range.
benefits: More of your gain taxed at lower rates
Can keep you under the extra 3.8% investment surtax
Steady payments plus interest income over the term
The payment schedule is a deal term you help set
steps: WE model the sale both ways and show you the savings from spreading it.
WE size the down payment so year-one taxes are covered with room to spare.
WE handle the installment tax form in the sale year and every collection year.
YOU have your attorney paper the note and security before closing.
clientCommitments: Track every payment you collect so each year’s tax filing is accurate
Tell us before changing, refinancing, or selling the note — those moves can trigger the deferred tax
